newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany fears missing EMU target in 1997 --paper.
newsitem.headline: Germany fears missing EMU target in 1997 --paper.

text.p: The German government is increasingly concerned it will not meet the strict restrictions on budget deficits this year needed to qualify for Europe's single currency, a daily newspaper reported on Friday.

Reacting to having overshot the 1996 target on new borrowing and an already higher-than-planned deficit this year, Finance Minister Theo Waigel will impose a public spending freeze this month, the economic daily Handelsblatt said.

The paper cited unnamed government sources and added that in his preparations for the annual report on the economy, to be released on January 28, Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt now assumes there will be 4.2 million jobless on average in 1997.
That figure exceeds the previous target by some 200,000 and could mean that the government will have to spend around six billion marks more for jobless benefits than expected.
Rexrodt is sticking to the government's real economic growth forecast of up to 2.5 percent this year. For next year, Rexrodt is forecasting 2-2.5 percent.
But the government expects nominal growth to suffer because of the favourable price climate. This will in turn lead to lower tax receipts.

As a result of these factors, Bonn no longer expects to meet its target of keeping the deficit to within 2.5 percent of gross domestic product and fears it could exceed the target for European economic and monetary union (EMU) altogether.
The Maastricht Treaty on EMU states that participants must keep budget deficits to no more than three percent of GDP and total public debt cannot exceed 60 percent of GDP.
The European Union will decide in 1998 which member states qualify for EMU the following year based on economic data from 1997.
